newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Jobs disaster buries Australia dlr at 16-mth lows.
newsitem.headline: Jobs disaster buries Australia dlr at 16-mth lows.

text.p: The Australian dollar dived to 16-month lows Thursday as disastrous jobs data forced the market to qestion its cosy assumptions of an economic recovery.

The 40,300 fall in employment came like a bolt from the blue as analysts had confidently expected a rise of around 15,000. The blow was softened on the crosses by a sudden and severe retreat in the yen, but analysts suspected it would prove only a temporary distraction from the heightened risk of a rate cut.
"There was nothing nice about these figures -- they were ugly all round," said Bruce Freeland chief economist at CBA.
"The odds of a rate cut have clearly increased and must now be in the 60 to 70 percent area," he said.
By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the dollar had sunk to US$0.7515/20, its lowest close since February 1996, from US$0.7564/69 before the data hit dealing screens and US$0.7590/95 late Wednesday.
On the crosses the situation was confused by a wild short covering rally in US$/yen which actually helped the local currency end firmer at 85.74/84 yen from 84.10/20 Wednesday.
The blistering bounce, which saw the U.S. dollar gain over four yen at one point, came when Japanese officials made clear their dissatifaction with the yen's recent rise.
It helped limit the local dollar's trade weighted losses to just 0.2 point at 57.1, when it had been as low as 56.8.
Nevertheless, the slide brought the dollar's fall to almost three cents since the Reserve Bank last cut rates on May 23 and dealers saw further pain ahead as the market priced in another.

The September 90-day bank bill, which most accurately reflects market thinking on where official rates are heading, leapt 22 basis points to 94.88. That implied a rate of 5.12 percent compared to the present 5.50 percent cash rate.
Money rates were now well below their U.S. equivalents meaning investors had to pay for the privilege of holding A$'s.

Many U.S. investors had already shown their displeasure with this novel situation -- the last time domestic rates were not above those in the U.S. was in the early 1980s -- and dealers suspected Japanese and European sellers would soon be testing 75 cent support.

Beneath there was a yawning gap on the charts from January 1996 when the dollar delved as deep as 73 cents before embarking on a steady rally to 80 cents in May. Some support was expected at US$0.7450 and US$0.7380, but analysts could not rule out a return to the 73 low if the RBA did indeed ease.
The risks seemed biased that way given the dire jobs data.

In defiance of all predictions employment fell 40,300 in May, the biggest monthly drop since April 1993, when the market had looked for a 15,000 rise. The unemployment rate ticked up just a basis point to 8.8 percent, but only because the number of people looking for work fell sharply. Without that, unemployment would have hit 9.3 percent.

"You can argue that unemployment is a lagging indicator and the forward indicators are pointing to jobs growth," Freeland at Commonwealth Bank. "But a figure as bad as this has implications for the economy now as it could well depress consumer sentiment and spending."
Some analysts felt there were enough signs of a pickup in critical areas of the economy to make the RBA pause until at least its next board meeting on July 1.

The outlook was also complicated by the impending Federal Reserve policy meeting on July 1-2 which could well sanction a rise in U.S. rates. Such a hike could make it hard to sustain another easing here by depressing the dollar and threatening imported inflation.
But given the RBA had surprised with three of its four cuts to date, it would be a brave man that ruled out an easing even as early as Friday morning. -- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
